questions.q: Perform a left shift of 2 places on the 8-bit number 00010110.
questions.feedback: 22 becomes 88: every bit moves two places left and zeros fill in from the right.
questions.hint: Shifting left multiplies. By how much, for each place?
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 10 — Shift and hex lab, station 1: Left shift

questions.q: Perform a right shift of 3 places on the 8-bit number 11000000.
questions.feedback: 192 becomes 24: every bit moves three places right.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 10 — Shift and hex lab, station 1: Left shift

questions.q: Explain what a left shift of 1 place does to the value of a binary number.

markPoints.concept: it doubles the value, or multiplies it by two
accept: double|doubles|multiplied by 2|multiply by 2|multiplied by two|multiply by two|times 2|x 2|twice

markPoints.concept: because every bit moves into a place worth twice as much
markPoints.exemplar: This is because every bit moves into a column worth twice as much.

questions.example: A left shift of one place doubles the value, because every bit moves into a place value worth twice as much as the one it was in.
questions.paraphrase: The number is multiplied by two, since each digit ends up in a column of double the worth.
questions.feedback: The effect, and why the effect is what it is.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 10 — Shift and hex lab, station 1: Left shift

questions.q: A right shift of 2 places is performed on the binary number 00001001 (9). What is lost?
options: The two least significant bits, so the answer is rounded down to 2
The two most significant bits, so the answer is far too small
Nothing; a right shift never loses anything
questions.feedback: 9 ÷ 4 is 2.25, but the bits that fall off the right-hand end are gone. The stored answer is 2.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 10 — Shift and hex lab, station 1: Left shift

questions.q: Explain why hexadecimal is often used to write down binary values.

markPoints.concept: it is much shorter than the equivalent binary
accept: short|shorter|fewer digits|fewer characters|compact|concise|two digits|2 digits|quarter of the space|less space|takes up less
markPoints.exemplar: A hex value is much shorter than the same value in binary.

markPoints.concept: so it is easier for people to read and less error-prone to copy
markPoints.exemplar: This makes it easier to read and less likely to be copied wrongly.

questions.example: Two hexadecimal digits say the same thing as eight binary digits, so it is far shorter, which makes it easier for a person to read and less likely that a digit is miscopied.
questions.paraphrase: It takes up a quarter of the space binary does, which means people can read it and copy it without losing their place.
questions.feedback: Shorter, therefore easier for a human. It is no easier for the computer, which works in binary either way.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 10 — Shift and hex lab, station 4: Why hexadecimal?

questions.q: Convert the denary number 202 to hexadecimal.
questions.feedback: 202 ÷ 16 = 12 remainder 10, so CA.
